title: LeetType Probe session (Oct 18 brief)
oneLine: A map and a primer card, three Paxos-to-Raft rounds where a struggle places a reading and parks the round, one spoken soundbite, then the parked round's return.

s_map.title: The map
s_map.body:
LeetType has two aims: motivate a systems design out loud, and get in the habit of reading the sources behind it.

Three skills:
Read: trace what a system does when something happens.
Speak: motivate a design choice out loud, then check yourself against a short rubric.
Conjugate: a force changes; pick the change that restores the budget or the invariant, and name the rule that decides.

Two sets of rules, Machine (8) and Agreement (10), walked in short threads. Today: Thread 1, From one value to a log. Next: Thread 2, The leader must fsync.

You have not walked any thread yet. The map shows threads in words, never a score.

s_rules.title: The rules on the map
s_rules.body:
Machine
M1 The latency ladder
M2 Batch to amortize a fixed cost
M3 Pointer chasing costs a miss per hop
M4 Little's law
M5 Shared writes serialize
M6 Queues explode near saturation
M7 Fan-out amplifies the tail
M8 Durability has a price

Agreement
A1 The failure model decides
A2 FLP: timeouts buy liveness, never safety
A3 Majorities intersect
A4 Safety always, liveness when stable
A5 A stable leader amortizes agreement
A6 Higher terms fence stale leaders
A7 Elect only complete leaders
A8 Committed means a majority stored it
A9 Replication is not consensus
A10 Reads need agreement too

s_primer.title: Today's new rule: A3, Majorities intersect
s_primer.body:
2f + 1 nodes tolerate f crashes, because any two majorities share a node that remembers.

With five nodes (f = 2) a majority is three. Any two groups of three out of five overlap in at least one node: 3 + 3 = 6, and there are only 5.

Today is Thread 1, From one value to a log: three rounds, then one soundbite where you speak. About 10 minutes. Each round states its job in one sentence at the top. If a round stumps you, you get a reading placed for it, not the answer.

r1.pinned: What may P2 propose in ballot 7?
r1.title: Round 1 · Read · Paxos
r1.body:
Single-decree Paxos, five acceptors A–E. Proposer P1 ran ballot 5; A, B and C accepted value x. Then P1 crashed before telling anyone. Proposer P2 runs ballot 7 and gets promises from C, D and E. C reports “I accepted (5, x)”. D and E report nothing.

Who holds what:
A, B, C: accepted (5, x)
D, E: nothing accepted
Promises to P2: C says (5, x); D and E say nothing

options.label: A. Its own value y: two of the three promises report nothing.
options.feedback: No answer here. A reading is placed instead, and this round is parked until you have read it.

options.label: B. Either value: ballot 7 outranks ballot 5, so both are safe.
options.feedback: No answer here. A reading is placed instead, and this round is parked until you have read it.

options.label: C. x: it must adopt the highest-ballot value any promise reports.
D. Nothing: a value is already chosen, so P2 must give up.
options.feedback: No answer here. A reading is placed instead, and this round is parked until you have read it.

options.label: Not sure
options.feedback: Noted as “Not sure”: that is evidence, not a miss. No answer here. A reading is placed instead, and this round is parked until you have read it.

ok1.title: Round 1: answered
ok1.body:
Right: C (A3, majorities intersect). x sits on a majority {A, B, C}, so it may already be chosen. Any majority P2 hears from shares at least one node with {A, B, C}, here C, and the rule says P2 must carry the highest-ballot value it hears.

A breaks the invariant: proposing y could choose a second value.
B confuses ordering with safety: the ballot only orders attempts (A6); what's carried forward is what makes it safe.
D: P2 can't know x is chosen (only C mentioned it). Proposing x is how it finishes safely; it doesn't give up.

p1.title: Why must any group P2 hears from include a node that remembers?
p1.primer: Round 1 is parked; no answer yet. Lamport picks a size for “large enough” and gives a one-line reason. Look for it: what would break if two such sets could be disjoint? Once you mark this read, Round 1 comes back in your next Probe session.
p1.passage: (Paraphrase; open the source for the paper's own words.) A value is chosen once a large enough set of acceptors has accepted it. Lamport takes “large enough” to mean any majority of the acceptors. His one-line reason: any two majorities have at least one acceptor in common, so if each acceptor accepts at most one value, two different values cannot both be chosen.

ok2.title: Round 2: answered
ok2.body:
Right: C (A5, a stable leader amortizes agreement). This is Multi-Paxos. Steady state is one accept round trip per entry ≈ 0.5 ms, and safety is the same as Round 1.

A breaks the budget: two round trips per entry, and competing proposers can livelock.
B fits the budget but breaks the invariant (A9): a write acknowledged before it reached a majority dies with the primary.
D breaks the invariant (A1, A2): clocks drift and timestamps tie, so two nodes can order the log differently.

p2.title: In a long log, which step does a leader repay for every entry, and which only once?
p2.primer: Round 2 is parked; no answer yet. Watch a stable leader run a whole log. Which phase does it pay per command, and which only once? Once you mark this read, Round 2 comes back in your next Probe session.
p2.passage: (Paraphrase; open the source for the paper's own words.) Section 3 turns the single-value algorithm into a log: one instance per command. A stable leader is elected as the distinguished proposer. Having one leader lets it run the first phase for all instances it has not started yet in a single step, so each later command costs only the second phase.

r3.pinned: S3 has just won the election for term 4. What happens to entry 7 on S2?
r3.title: Round 3 · Read · Raft
r3.body:
Five Raft servers, S1–S5. Entries 1–6 (all term 3) are committed on every server. Leader S1 (term 3) appends entry 7, replicates it to S2 only, then crashes. No client has had an answer for entry 7. S3 times out first and asks for votes in term 4.

Who holds what:
Entries 1–6 (term 3): all five servers
Entry 7 (term 3): S1 and S2 only
S3's log ends at entry 6. S1 is down.

options.label: A. S3 first copies entry 7 from S2, since S2 has the longer log.
options.feedback: No answer here. A reading is placed instead, and this round is parked until you have read it.

options.label: B. It gets overwritten: entry 7 was never committed, and no client was told it was.
C. It stays: Raft never deletes an entry once a server has stored it.
options.feedback: No answer here. A reading is placed instead, and this round is parked until you have read it.

options.label: D. The premise is impossible: S2 refuses its vote, so S3 can't reach a majority.

ok3.title: Round 3: answered
ok3.body:
Right: B (A7, A8). S2 refuses its vote, because its log (index 7, term 3) is more up to date than S3's. S4 and S5 grant theirs, so S3 wins with three of five. Entry 7 was only on two servers, so it was never committed, and the new leader's log overwrites it on S2.

A: in Raft, data flows only from leader to follower. Elections are restricted precisely so that a winner never needs to fetch anything.
C: uncommitted entries on followers are overwritten when they conflict with the leader.
D: one refusal isn't a lost majority.

p3.title: How does a voter decide whose log is more up to date, and what does that guarantee about the winner?
p3.primer: Round 3 is parked; no answer yet. How does a voter compare logs, and what does the restriction guarantee about any winner? Once you mark this read, Round 3 comes back in your next Probe session.

source.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (extended)
source.author: Ongaro, Ousterhout

p3.passage: (Paraphrase; open the source for the paper's own words.) A server grants its vote only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date as its own. Up to date is compared on the last entry: a later term wins; with equal terms, the longer log wins. A committed entry sits on a majority and a winner needs a majority, so at least one voter holds every committed entry. The winner's log therefore already contains all of them.

rec.pinned: In 45 seconds, out loud: why did Raft's authors bother, given Multi-Paxos?
rec.title: Round 4 · Speak · why Raft?
rec.body: Tap to record, and tap again to stop, up to 60 seconds. The rubric appears only after you have recorded. Your recording is kept with its prompt, rubric and ticks, and exported to Drive for the weekly review.
rec.prompt: Multi-Paxos already replicates a log with a stable leader. In 45 seconds, out loud: why did Raft's authors bother?
rubric: Understandability was the explicit goal: published Multi-Paxos leaves leader election, gaps in the log and catch-up to each implementer, and implementations diverge.
A strong leader: entries flow only from leader to followers, with no per-slot recovery of values from acceptors.
The election restriction: only a candidate with an up-to-date log can win, so a new leader already has every committed entry (A7).
Fewer states to reason about: terms, plus the log-matching property (same index and term means the same history up to there).

p4.title: What was the complaint about Paxos that Raft was built to answer?
p4.primer: Your soundbite is parked; the self-check is the strongest sign of a gap. Before deciding whether Raft is “Paxos made easy”, read the complaint. It's about which subproblem Paxos was built on. Once you mark this read, the soundbite comes back in your next Probe session.

source.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (extended)
source.author: Ongaro, Ousterhout

p4.passage: (Paraphrase; open the source for the paper's own words.) Section 3 says Paxos has two drawbacks. It is exceptionally difficult to understand. And it is a poor foundation for building practical systems: the single-decree protocol is subtle, and there is no widely agreed algorithm for multi-Paxos, so implementations diverge from it. The authors made understandability an explicit goal of Raft.
